title: Breathlessness after a 20 km run in a 20-year-old man
desc: This station is a focused breathlessness history and a full respiratory examination of Sam Jones, a 20-year-old university student seeing his GP. He became short of breath during his first 20 km run and it has now settled. Every examination finding is normal. In Part 2 the candidate interprets his observations, a chest X-ray report and spirometry, all of which are normal. They should conclude that this is physiological exertional breathlessness after an unaccustomed run, explain why pneumothorax, pulmonary embolism, cardiac disease and exercise-induced bronchoconstriction are unlikely or not yet excluded, name the investigations used for breathlessness, say when a V/Q scan is preferred over a CTPA, and safety-net.
focus: A complete, systematic respiratory examination in a well young man with exertional breathlessness, then interpreting normal results, ruling out the dangerous causes and choosing investigations
stem: You are a medical student on placement in a general practice. Sam Jones is a 20-year-old man who has come into the clinic today because he became very short of breath towards the end of a 20 km run this morning. Your supervising GP has asked you to see him first and is available in the next room.
tasks: Take a focused history from Sam and perform a full respiratory examination, telling the examiner what you are examining and why (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you his observations, chest X-ray report and spirometry. Give an ISBAR handover that interprets them, state your most likely diagnosis and differentials, outline your management and safety netting, and answer a question on investigations (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Sam Jones, a 20-year-old second-year engineering student. Your date of birth is 14 March 2006. You are tall and slim, relaxed, and a bit embarrassed to be at the doctor. You are breathing comfortably now, speak in full sentences and look well. You are happy to take your shirt off for the examination. When the candidate says what they would examine, the examiner gives the findings from the Exam findings below.

Opening line: "I went for a 20 k run this morning and got really puffed, worse than I've ever been. My housemate told me I should get it checked."

The breathlessness (give only when asked):

  • When: this morning. You set off at about 6:30 and ran for about 2 hours on a mild, sunny morning.
  • Context: you are training for your first half marathon (21.1 km), which is in 4 weeks. You usually run 8 to 10 km three times a week. Your longest run before today was 12 km, two weeks ago. Today was the first time you had tried 20 km.
  • Onset and course: it came on gradually over the last 5 km or so. You were breathing very hard and fast and "just couldn't get enough air in". It eased once you slowed to a walk for the last 2 km and you were breathing normally within about 10 minutes of stopping.
  • Now: you feel back to normal when you are sitting still, just tired, with sore legs.
  • Previous episodes: never like this. You get puffed on hard runs like anyone, but it has never stopped you before. You are never breathless at rest or at night.

Other symptoms (only if asked; all absent unless stated):

  • Heart: no chest pain or tightness, no racing or irregular heartbeat, no dizziness or light-headedness, no fainting or collapse.
  • Lungs: no wheeze or whistling, no cough during or after the run, no sharp pain on breathing in, no sudden pain on one side of the chest, no coughing up blood. No noisy or high-pitched sound when breathing in and no tightness in the throat.
  • Clots: no calf pain or swelling. No long flights or car trips, no operations, injuries or time laid up in bed. No clots before.
  • Infection: no recent cold or flu, no fever, no sore throat.
  • Heat and fluids: you took a 750 mL water bottle and drank it, plus water at home. No vomiting, confusion or cramps. You passed urine normally afterwards.
  • Airways (only if asked about allergies, hay fever or asthma): you get hay fever in spring (sneezing, itchy eyes) and sometimes take a loratadine tablet from the chemist. "Mum says I never had asthma as a kid." No eczema. You have not noticed that cold air or particular seasons affect your breathing.

Past medical history: nothing apart from hay fever. No operations, never in hospital.

Medications: loratadine 10 mg when your hay fever is bad (none this week). You have a whey protein shake after training. If asked: no pre-workout or other supplements, no steroids or other performance-enhancing drugs, no recreational drugs.

Allergies: none. If asked about X-ray dye: you have never had any.

Family history: your parents are well; your dad takes a tablet for high cholesterol. If asked: no one in your family has died suddenly or young, had a heart problem as a young person, or had blood clots. No one has asthma.

Social history: you live in a share house near the university and work part-time in a café. You have never smoked or vaped. You drink about 4 to 6 beers on a weekend night.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you wonder whether you have asthma. Your main worry is that you won't be able to run the half marathon, which you are raising money for. You would like to know whether it is safe to keep training.

Question to raise (near the end of Part 1, if not already covered): "Do you reckon it's asthma?"

Exam findings (the examiner gives these only when the candidate says what they would examine):

  • General: tall, slim young man sitting comfortably with his shirt off. Pink, not distressed, speaking in full sentences. No inhaler, spacer or oxygen with him. Height 186 cm, weight 72 kg (BMI 20.8).
  • Vital signs (10:20): HR 68 beats/min, regular; BP 122/74 mmHg; RR 14/min; SpO2 99% on room air; temperature 36.8 °C.
  • Pulsus paradoxus: not present (the systolic pressure falls by less than 10 mmHg on inspiration).
  • Hands: warm and pink. No peripheral cyanosis, clubbing or tar staining. No wasting of the small muscles; finger abduction strength normal. No asterixis. No wrist tenderness. No fine tremor.
  • Face: no frontal or maxillary sinus tenderness.
  • Eyes: no conjunctival pallor, no scleral icterus, no ptosis or miosis (no Horner's syndrome).
  • Nose: turbinates not engorged, septum midline, no polyps.
  • Mouth: with torch and tongue depressor: pharynx not crowded, no ulcers, tonsils not enlarged. No central cyanosis.
  • Neck: no cervical or supraclavicular lymph nodes. Trachea midline, no tracheal tug. Pemberton's sign negative. JVP not raised.
  • Chest inspection: no scars or rashes, no swelling. Symmetrical, with no pectus excavatum or carinatum, barrel chest, Harrison's sulcus, kyphosis or scoliosis. Hoover's sign absent.
  • Chest palpation: no rib tenderness, no subcutaneous emphysema. Apex beat in the 5th intercostal space, midclavicular line. Chest expansion 6 cm and symmetrical.
  • Percussion: resonant throughout, anteriorly from the clavicles (including the apices), laterally and posteriorly, equal on both sides.
  • Auscultation: normal vesicular breath sounds anteriorly, laterally and posteriorly, with no added sounds (no wheeze, crackles or rub). Vocal resonance normal and symmetrical.
  • Cardiovascular (if the candidate says they would complete with it): pulse regular, heart sounds dual with no murmurs, including on standing if asked.
  • Legs: no swelling, oedema or calf tenderness; calves equal in size.
  • Peak flow or spirometry: "These will be given to you in Part 2."

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self as a medical student, confirms Sam's name and date of birth, explains the history and examination and gains consent.
Exposes the chest appropriately (shirt removed, offers a chaperone) and positions Sam seated and comfortable, asking about pain first.
check.d: Source preliminary marks: shirt removed, seated, comfortable.

check.x: Opens with an open question, uses plain language, acknowledges his worry about the half marathon, and thanks him and offers help to dress at the end.
History
Characterises the breathlessness:

kids.x: Onset and context: came on gradually over the last 5 km of his first 20 km run this morning; usually runs 8 to 10 km, and his longest run before today was 12 km.
Severity and course: had to slow to a walk for the last 2 km; it eased with walking and he was breathing normally within about 10 minutes of stopping; now back to normal at rest.
Previous episodes: none on his usual runs; no breathlessness at rest or at night.

check.x: Screens for a cardiac cause:

kids.x: Asks about chest pain, palpitations, dizziness, and fainting or collapse during exercise (all absent).
Asks about a family history of sudden death or heart disease at a young age (none).
kids.d: Credit if asked in the family history.

check.x: Screens for pneumothorax and pulmonary embolism: sudden or sharp pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, calf pain or swelling, and VTE risk factors (long travel, immobility, surgery or injury, previous clot) (all absent).
check.d: Credit with at least pleuritic pain, haemoptysis or leg symptoms, and at least two VTE risk factors.

check.x: Screens for airway disease and infection: wheeze, cough or chest tightness during or after exercise, triggers such as cold air, childhood asthma, atopy, and recent viral illness or fever. Finds seasonal hay fever only and no recent illness.
check.d: Hay fever is given only if allergies, hay fever or asthma are asked about.

check.x: Asks about PMH, medications including supplements or performance-enhancing drugs, allergies, and smoking or vaping (hay fever, loratadine when needed, whey protein, no allergies, never smoked).
check.d: Alcohol, accommodation and work are uncredited extras.

check.x: Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations: he wonders whether it is asthma, is worried about missing the half marathon and wants to know whether he can keep training.
Examination
General inspection: aids (inhaler, spacer, oxygen), body habitus (tall and slim), colour and distress, and whether he speaks in full sentences.
Asks for vital signs: BP, HR, RR, SpO2 and temperature (all normal).
check.d: RR and SpO2 must be included. Pulsus paradoxus is not required.

check.x: Examines the hands: peripheral cyanosis, clubbing and tar staining; small muscle wasting and weak finger abduction (apical (Pancoast) tumour); wrist tenderness (hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy); asterixis (hypercapnia) and fine tremor (excess salbutamol).
check.d: Credit with clubbing, cyanosis and one other hand sign.

check.x: States they would examine the face, eyes, nose and mouth (e.g. Horner's syndrome, pallor, nasal polyps, pharynx).
check.d: Credit with any two areas named; a torch and tongue depressor are not required.

check.x: Examines the neck: cervical lymph nodes in all groups including supraclavicular, tracheal position and tracheal tug, Pemberton's sign, and mentions the JVP.
check.d: Critical element: tracheal position. A deviated trachea would point to tension pneumothorax or collapse.

check.x: Inspects the chest: scars, rashes, swelling and symmetry, and chest wall deformity (Harrison's sulcus, pectus excavatum or carinatum, barrel chest, kyphosis, scoliosis).
Palpates the chest: rib tenderness, subcutaneous emphysema, apex beat, and chest expansion (6 cm and symmetrical; normal is more than 5 cm).
check.d: Critical elements: subcutaneous emphysema and symmetry of expansion. Vocal fremitus is not needed.

check.x: Percusses from the clavicles (including the apices) downwards, comparing left with right, and the back with his arms crossed (resonant throughout).
Auscultates anteriorly, laterally and posteriorly with him breathing through the mouth, comparing sides, and tests vocal resonance. Reports normal vesicular breath sounds with no added sounds.
Examines the legs for DVT: swelling, oedema and calf tenderness (none).
States they would complete the examination with a cardiovascular examination, peak flow and spirometry.
Interpretation
Observations: normal and stable at both sets (SpO2 99% on room air, RR 14, afebrile), with a resting HR of 62 to 68 in keeping with a trained runner.
Chest X-ray: normal, and specifically no pneumothorax (lung markings to the periphery, no visible pleural edge), no consolidation or effusion, normal heart size.
check.d: Stating that a pneumothorax has been excluded is the critical element.

check.x: Spirometry: normal, with FEV1/FVC 0.84 (above the lower limit of normal) and FEV1 99% predicted, and no significant bronchodilator response (+120 mL, 2.5%; significant is at least 12% and at least 200 mL). States that normal resting spirometry does not exclude exercise-induced bronchoconstriction.
check.d: Credit "no significant bronchodilator response" without the numbers; FEV1/FVC above the LLN and the statement that normal spirometry does not exclude EIB are required.

check.x: States the most likely diagnosis: physiological exertional breathlessness after an unaccustomed 20 km run, now resolved. Justifies it with the big jump in distance, the gradual onset and settling within about 10 minutes of stopping, no red-flag symptoms, and a normal examination and results.

Gives at least three differentials, each with a feature against it: exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (no wheeze, cough or tightness, normal spirometry, but not excluded), exercise-induced laryngeal obstruction (difficulty getting air in at peak effort, but no stridor or throat tightness; not excluded by a normal resting flow-volume loop), primary spontaneous pneumothorax (normal chest signs and X-ray), pulmonary embolism (no risk factors, PERC negative), cardiac disease (no chest pain, palpitations, syncope or family history, normal heart examination; a resting ECG today is reasonable).
check.d: Critical standard: addresses both pneumothorax and PE, each with a feature against it. Full credit needs at least three differentials.

check.x: Management

Explains in plain words that his examination, X-ray and breathing test are normal and that he pushed further than his training had prepared him for, answers his asthma question honestly, and answers his half-marathon question: he can aim for it, building up gradually, warming up, keeping up fluids and stopping if symptoms return.
Does not order a D-dimer or CTPA; if PE is discussed, justifies this with low pretest probability and PERC negative.
check.d: Fail only if the candidate orders a D-dimer or CTPA.

check.x: States that if cough, wheeze or chest tightness come with exercise he should return for a bronchial provocation test before any inhaler is started; that recurrent or disproportionate exertional breathlessness needs GP review with ECG and echocardiography (cardiology review if abnormal); and that a resting 12-lead ECG can be done in the practice today.
check.d: Credit a candidate who arranges a resting 12-lead ECG now, given his exertional symptoms.

check.x: Names at least four investigations for breathlessness beyond bedside tests and bloods: chest X-ray, CTPA, V/Q scan, spirometry, HRCT, lung biopsy, point-of-care lung and cardiac ultrasound (eFAST in trauma).
check.d: Source marking: full marks for four. Also accept FAST, echocardiography or bronchial provocation testing.

check.x: States that a V/Q scan is preferred over a CTPA in contrast allergy and in pregnancy.
check.d: Both are needed. Renal impairment is also credited but not required.

check.x: Safety netting

Gives red flags in plain words with the action. Call 000: chest pain, fainting or collapse, sudden one-sided chest pain with breathlessness, breathlessness at rest, or breathlessness that is worse than today's or does not settle within 15 minutes of stopping.
check.d: Credit at least three specific red flags linked to calling 000.

check.x: Tells him to see a GP or go to ED the same day for coughing up blood, and arranges GP review in 2 to 3 weeks, before the race.

part2.lead: Sam had a chest X-ray at the radiology practice next door and spirometry with the practice nurse. It is now 11:45. Here are his observations, his chest X-ray report and his spirometry results.
part2.patient:
Sam is present for question 3. When the candidate explains, he asks, if not already covered: "Can I still do the half marathon in 4 weeks?"

He is relieved by a clear explanation and a plan for what to do if it happens again.

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Taken by the practice nurse on room air: at 10:20 on arrival and at 11:40 on his return from X-ray and spirometry.
handover.model:
Read: at both sets HR 62 to 68 regular, BP 120 to 122/72 to 74, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 to 36.8 °C, alert, no pain, no distress.

For Sam: completely normal and stable observations. Every value would sit in the normal (white) zone of an adult observation chart such as the NSW Between the Flags chart. A resting heart rate in the 60s fits a fit young runner. A heart rate under 100 and SpO2 of 95% or more are also two of the PERC criteria.

What it changes: nothing here calls for urgent action or transfer, so he is safe to go home with advice and safety netting.

rows.note: Repeat set on return from X-ray and spirometry

handover.label: Chest X-ray report
handover.result:
Examination: chest X-ray, PA erect, taken at 10:55 today. Sam Jones, 20.

Clinical details: 20-year-old man, tall and slim, with acute breathlessness during a 20 km run this morning, now settled. Normal examination. Exclude pneumothorax.

Comparison: no previous imaging.

Technique: not rotated. Adequate inspiration (6 anterior ribs above the right hemidiaphragm in the midclavicular line). Adequate exposure.

Findings:

  • Soft tissues and bones: normal. No rib fracture. No subcutaneous emphysema.
  • Airway and mediastinum: trachea central. Mediastinum not widened. Both hila normal in size and position.
  • Lungs: clear. Lung markings extend to the chest wall on both sides, including the apices. No consolidation, nodule or mass. No hyperinflation.
  • Pleura: no visible pleural edge and no pneumothorax. No pleural effusion.
  • Heart: normal size (cardiothoracic ratio below 0.5), normal heart borders.
  • Diaphragm: both hemidiaphragms normal in position and outline. Costophrenic angles sharp. No free gas under the diaphragm.
  • Lines and devices: none.

Conclusion: normal chest X-ray. No pneumothorax.
handover.model:
Read (DRSABCDE): correct patient and date, PA erect, not rotated, adequate inspiration and exposure. Soft tissues and bones normal, no surgical emphysema. Trachea central, mediastinum and hila normal. Lungs clear, with markings to the periphery and the apices, and no hyperinflation. No pleural edge, pneumothorax or effusion. Heart size normal. Diaphragms and costophrenic angles normal, no free gas. No lines.

For Sam: a primary spontaneous pneumothorax was the main structural concern in a tall, slim young man with acute breathlessness, and this film excludes one of any significance. It also shows no consolidation and no signs of heart disease.

What it changes: no further imaging is needed. A normal X-ray does not exclude PE, but his clinical probability of PE is low.

handover.label: Spirometry with bronchodilator response
handover.result:
Spirometry with bronchodilator response, performed by the practice nurse at 11:15 today. Sam Jones, 20, male. Height 186 cm, weight 72 kg. Predicted values: GLI-2012.

Technique: 3 acceptable and repeatable manoeuvres before and after bronchodilator, with good effort. Bronchodilator: salbutamol 400 micrograms via spacer, retested 15 minutes later.

FEV14.78 L99%3.98 L4.90 L+120 mL (+2.5%)
FVC5.71 L98%4.80 L5.76 L+50 mL (+1%)

Flow-volume loop: normal shape, with no scooping of the expiratory limb and no flattening of the inspiratory or expiratory limb.

Report: spirometry within normal limits. No significant bronchodilator response.
handover.model:
Read: good-quality test. FEV1/FVC 0.84 is above the lower limit of normal, so there is no airflow obstruction. FEV1 and FVC are normal (98 to 99% predicted), so there is no restrictive pattern. After salbutamol FEV1 rose by 120 mL (2.5%), which is not significant: in adults a significant response is an increase of at least 12% and at least 200 mL. The flow-volume loop is normal, with no flattening to suggest upper airway obstruction at rest (a normal resting loop does not exclude exercise-induced laryngeal obstruction).

For Sam: there is no evidence of asthma at rest. However, normal resting spirometry does not exclude exercise-induced bronchoconstriction, which is confirmed with a bronchial provocation test (for example an exercise or mannitol challenge).

What it changes: objective confirmation is preferred before starting an inhaler. If symptoms suggesting bronchoconstriction come back with exercise, he should return for provocation testing.

ask: Your supervising GP has come back into the room. Please give an ISBAR handover of Sam, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Sam now, here in general practice, including what you would tell him and the follow-up you would arrange before he goes home.
Besides bedside tests and blood tests, what other investigations can be used to assess a patient with shortness of breath, and when is a V/Q scan preferred over a CTPA?
expect:
• Identify: self, medical student. Sam Jones, 20, university student.
  • Situation: marked breathlessness towards the end of a 20 km run this morning, now resolved. Normal examination and results.
  • Background: first 20 km run (longest before 12 km); eased on walking and settled within about 10 minutes of stopping. No cardiac, pleuritic, VTE or airway red flags, no family history of sudden death, hay fever only, non-smoker.
  • Assessment: observations normal and stable (HR 62, RR 14, SpO2 99% on air, BP 120/72, afebrile). Full respiratory examination normal. Chest X-ray normal, with no pneumothorax. Spirometry normal (FEV1/FVC 0.84, FEV1 99%) with no significant bronchodilator response. Probable physiological exertional breathlessness; PERC negative; exercise-induced bronchoconstriction not excluded.
  • Recommendation: home today with training advice and safety netting. Resting 12-lead ECG in the practice today. Bronchial provocation test if exercise symptoms come with cough, wheeze or tightness; ECG and echo review if breathlessness recurs. Please review him with me.

Most likely: physiological exertional breathlessness after an unaccustomed 20 km run, now resolved. For it: a big jump in distance, gradual onset late in the run that settled within about 10 minutes of stopping, no red-flag symptoms, and a normal examination, X-ray and spirometry.

  • Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction: for it: hay fever, and it is spring, his hay fever season. Against it: no wheeze, cough or tightness, and normal spirometry, which does not exclude it.
  • EILO: inspiratory difficulty at peak effort; not excluded by a normal resting loop.
  • Primary spontaneous pneumothorax: for it: tall, slim young man. Against it: no pleuritic pain, symmetrical expansion, resonant, normal breath sounds, normal X-ray.
  • Pulmonary embolism: against it: no risk factors, resolved, PERC negative.
  • Cardiac disease (cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia): against it: no chest pain, palpitations, syncope or family history, normal heart examination; a resting ECG today is reasonable.

1. Explain: his examination, X-ray and breathing test are normal; he ran much further than his training had prepared him for. Asthma is not shown at rest but cannot be fully excluded. He can go home today (discuss with the GP).
  2. No D-dimer or CTPA (low pretest probability, PERC negative); a resting 12-lead ECG can be done in the practice today.
  3. Training and recurrence: he can still aim for the half marathon if he builds up gradually, warms up, keeps up fluids and stops if symptoms return; if it recurs with cough, wheeze or tightness, a bronchial provocation test before any inhaler.
  4. Red flags and follow-up: call 000 for chest pain, fainting or collapse, sudden one-sided chest pain with breathlessness, or breathlessness at rest, worse than today's or not settling within 15 minutes of stopping. Same-day GP or ED review for coughing up blood. GP review in 2 to 3 weeks, before the race.

• Investigations (at least four): chest X-ray, CTPA, V/Q scan, spirometry. (Other answers credited under item 34: HRCT, lung biopsy, point-of-care lung and cardiac ultrasound, FAST/eFAST, echocardiography, bronchial provocation testing.)
  • V/Q preferred over CTPA: contrast allergy; pregnancy.

ddx.dx: Physiological exertional breathlessness after an unaccustomed 20 km run
ddx.for: His first 20 km run after a longest run of 12 km, gradual onset late in the run that eased on walking and settled within about 10 minutes of stopping, no red-flag symptoms, and a normal examination, X-ray and spirometry.
ddx.against: The breathlessness was bad enough that he had to walk and came to see a doctor.

ddx.for: Breathlessness with exercise in a young man with seasonal hay fever, and it is currently spring, his hay fever season.
ddx.against: No wheeze, cough or chest tightness, no childhood asthma, and normal spirometry with no bronchodilator response (which does not exclude it).

ddx.for: Difficulty getting air in at peak effort in a young athlete, with no bronchodilator response.
ddx.against: No stridor or throat tightness, though a normal resting flow-volume loop does not exclude it (it is confirmed by continuous laryngoscopy during exercise).

ddx.for: Acute breathlessness in a tall, slim young man.
ddx.against: No pleuritic or one-sided chest pain, symmetrical expansion, resonant percussion, normal breath sounds and no pneumothorax on the X-ray.
No VTE risk factors, no leg symptoms or haemoptysis, symptoms fully resolved, normal observations and PERC negative.

ddx.dx: Structural heart disease or arrhythmia (for example hypertrophic cardiomyopathy)
ddx.for: Exertional symptoms in a young endurance athlete.
ddx.against: No chest pain, palpitations, dizziness or syncope, no family history of sudden death, and a normal heart examination with a regular pulse; a resting ECG today is reasonable.

guide:
In Part 1, the source is an examination station, and every finding is normal. Give the findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they would examine. Give hay fever only if allergies, hay fever or asthma are asked about. Keep the candidate moving: about 4 minutes on the history and 6 on the examination; the examiner gives each finding briefly and moves the candidate on. Items 15 to 23 follow the source's examination marks (peripheral examination, chest, and completing with a cardiovascular examination, peak flow and spirometry). Credit each item only when the candidate says or does it. A candidate who performs the manoeuvres silently should be prompted once to say what they are looking for. Vocal fremitus and whispering pectoriloquy are not needed. If the candidate asks for peak flow or spirometry in Part 1, say that it will be given in Part 2.

In Part 2, hand over all three results together and ask the four questions in order. Sam puts his question during question 3 if the candidate has not covered it. Question 4 is the source's own pair of examiner questions. The source accepts FAST in its list, so credit it, along with point-of-care lung and cardiac ultrasound. Credit item 29 (the differentials) in the ISBAR or the diagnosis answer, and item 32 in any answer. Credit a candidate who would arrange a resting 12-lead ECG because of his exertional symptoms (item 33).

A high-performing candidate takes a brief, targeted history that screens for cardiac, pneumothorax, PE and airway causes, including the family history of sudden death. They perform a fluent, complete respiratory examination, narrating each step, and compare sides throughout. In Part 2 they confirm that the X-ray excludes a pneumothorax, read the spirometry correctly (noting that it does not exclude exercise-induced bronchoconstriction), avoid unnecessary PE investigation, give practical training advice and specific red flags, and answer the investigation questions crisply.

A borderline candidate skips the history to examine, omits the trachea, the back of the chest or the legs, or examines without comparing sides. They may start a salbutamol inhaler on the basis of hay fever alone, order a D-dimer or CTPA without a reason, or send him off with "come back if worried".
explain:
Diagnosis: physiological exertional breathlessness, with a normal respiratory examination

Sam is a fit 20-year-old who increased his longest run by two-thirds, from 12 km to 20 km, in two weeks. His breathlessness came on gradually over the last 5 km, eased when he slowed to a walk, and settled within about 10 minutes of stopping. He has no chest pain, palpitations, syncope, pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, wheeze or cough. He has no VTE risk factors and no family history of sudden death. His examination, observations, chest X-ray and spirometry are all normal. The most likely explanation is that he exercised beyond his current fitness. The skill being tested is to examine thoroughly and systematically, recognise that the findings are normal, and use the history and a few simple tests to exclude the causes that must not be missed, without over-investigating.

The respiratory examination

  • Preliminaries: hand hygiene, introduction and consent, shirt removed, patient seated and comfortable.
  • General inspection: aids (inhalers, spacer, oxygen), body habitus (a tall, slim build is a risk factor for primary spontaneous pneumothorax), colour and distress.
  • Vital signs: BP, HR, RR, SpO2 and temperature. Pulsus paradoxus (a fall in systolic pressure of more than 10 mmHg on inspiration) suggests severe asthma or cardiac tamponade.
  • Hands: peripheral cyanosis, clubbing, tar staining, small muscle wasting and weakness of finger abduction (lower brachial plexus involvement by an apical tumour), wrist tenderness (hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy), asterixis (hypercapnia) and fine tremor (excess salbutamol).
  • Face and head: sinus tenderness; eyes for anaemia, jaundice and Horner's syndrome; nose for engorged turbinates, a deviated septum and polyps; mouth for a crowded pharynx (obstructive sleep apnoea), ulcers and enlarged tonsils, using a torch and tongue depressor.
  • Neck: all cervical node groups, including supraclavicular; tracheal deviation and tracheal tug; Pemberton's sign (facial plethora on raising the arms, from a retrosternal goitre or SVC obstruction); JVP.
  • Chest:
    • Inspection: scars, rashes, swelling, symmetry and deformity (Harrison's sulcus from childhood asthma, pectus excavatum or carinatum, barrel chest, kyphosis, scoliosis), and Hoover's sign (paradoxical indrawing of the lower ribs in hyperinflation).
    • Palpation: rib tenderness, subcutaneous emphysema, apex beat and expansion (normally more than 5 cm).
    • Percussion: from the clavicles down, comparing left with right, and the back with the arms crossed.
    • Auscultation: with the patient breathing through the mouth, anteriorly, laterally and posteriorly, plus vocal resonance.
  • Legs: signs of DVT.
  • To complete: cardiovascular examination, peak flow and spirometry.

The differentials that matter

  • Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction: causes cough, wheeze, chest tightness or breathlessness during or, typically, shortly after exercise. Atopy (his hay fever, and it is currently spring) increases the likelihood. Resting spirometry is often normal, so a normal result does not exclude it. The Australian Asthma Handbook recommends confirming it objectively, with a bronchial provocation test (exercise challenge, or an indirect challenge such as mannitol), rather than labelling it on symptoms alone.
  • Exercise-induced laryngeal obstruction: narrowing at the larynx at high exercise intensity causes difficulty breathing in, sometimes with inspiratory stridor or throat tightness, and settles soon after exercise stops. It occurs in young athletes, is often mistaken for asthma and does not respond to a bronchodilator. A normal resting flow-volume loop does not exclude it; it is confirmed by continuous laryngoscopy during exercise. Sam's difficulty getting air in at peak effort is one reason not to label him asthmatic on symptoms alone.
  • Primary spontaneous pneumothorax: typically sudden pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness in a tall, thin young man (smoking increases the risk). Look for reduced expansion, hyper-resonance and reduced breath sounds on one side, and tracheal deviation in tension. The chest X-ray is the first test.
  • Pulmonary embolism: unlikely here. When clinical probability is low, PERC can be used: age under 50, HR under 100, SpO2 of 95% or more, no haemoptysis, no oestrogen use, no previous VTE, no unilateral leg swelling, and no recent surgery or trauma needing hospital care. If all are met, no D-dimer or imaging is needed. Sam meets every criterion.
  • Cardiac causes in young athletes: hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, other cardiomyopathies and arrhythmias can present with exertional breathlessness, chest pain, palpitations or syncope. Always ask about exertional syncope and a family history of sudden death or heart disease at a young age. A resting 12-lead ECG is reasonable in any young athlete with exertional symptoms; echocardiography and cardiology review are needed if the ECG is abnormal or there is exertional chest pain, palpitations, syncope, a family history of sudden death, or breathlessness that recurs or is out of proportion to the exertion.

Interpreting the results

  • Observations: normal and stable. A resting HR in the 60s is expected in a trained runner.
  • Chest X-ray: read systematically (DRSABCDE). In a suspected pneumothorax, look for a visible pleural edge with no lung markings beyond it, especially at the apices. Sam's film is normal.
  • Spirometry: an FEV1/FVC above the lower limit of normal excludes airflow obstruction. A normal FVC makes restriction unlikely. A significant bronchodilator response in adults is an FEV1 increase of at least 12% and at least 200 mL (Australian Asthma Handbook). Sam's result is normal with no significant response.

Investigations for breathlessness

Beyond bedside tests (observations, peak flow, ECG) and bloods (FBC, UEC, D-dimer, troponin, BNP, blood gas), other investigations include:

  • chest X-ray;
  • CTPA;
  • V/Q scan;
  • spirometry, with bronchodilator response and bronchial provocation where needed;
  • HRCT for interstitial lung disease;
  • lung biopsy;
  • point-of-care lung and cardiac ultrasound (eFAST in trauma).

Echocardiography is the key test when a cardiac cause is suspected.

V/Q scan or CTPA

CTPA is the usual first-line imaging for suspected PE: it is widely available and can show other diagnoses. A V/Q scan avoids iodinated contrast, so it is preferred in contrast allergy (and in significant renal impairment). In pregnancy, a V/Q (or perfusion-only) scan gives a lower radiation dose to the maternal breast, although local protocols vary. A V/Q scan is most reliable when the chest X-ray is normal, because lung disease makes the scan harder to interpret.

Management and safety netting

Sam can go home. Explain that his examination and tests are normal, and that the most likely cause is that he ran much further than his training had prepared him for. He can still aim for the half marathon: advise him to build up his distance gradually before the race, warm up, keep up fluids, and stop and rest if symptoms recur. He does not need an inhaler, a D-dimer or a CTPA; a resting 12-lead ECG can be done in the practice today. Echocardiography and cardiology review are needed if the ECG is abnormal or he develops chest pain, palpitations or fainting on exercise. If cough, wheeze or chest tightness come with exercise, he should return for bronchial provocation testing before any inhaler is started; if the breathlessness recurs or is out of proportion to the exertion, he needs review with echocardiography. Give brief advice that 4 to 6 full-strength beers (about 5.5 to 8.5 standard drinks) exceeds the NHMRC limit of 4 standard drinks on any day, and is worth cutting back while training.

He should call 000 for:

  • chest pain;
  • fainting or collapse;
  • sudden one-sided chest pain with breathlessness;
  • breathlessness at rest, or breathlessness that is worse than today's or does not settle within 15 minutes of stopping.

He should see a GP or go to ED the same day for coughing up blood.

Book a GP review in 2 to 3 weeks, before the half marathon (sooner if symptoms recur).
points: A respiratory examination is systematic: general inspection, vital signs, hands, face, neck, chest (inspection, palpation, percussion, auscultation, front, side and back, comparing sides) and legs, completed with a cardiovascular examination, peak flow and spirometry.

In a young person with exertional breathlessness, always screen for the dangerous causes: pneumothorax (sudden pleuritic pain, tall slim build), PE (risk factors, PERC) and cardiac disease (exertional chest pain, palpitations, syncope, family history of sudden death).
A low pretest probability with all PERC criteria met means no D-dimer or CTPA is needed. Avoid investigations that add radiation and contrast without changing management.

Normal resting spirometry does not exclude exercise-induced bronchoconstriction. Confirm it with a bronchial provocation test rather than starting an inhaler on suspicion alone. In adults, a significant bronchodilator response is an FEV1 increase of at least 12% and at least 200 mL.

Investigations for breathlessness beyond bedside tests and bloods include chest X-ray, CTPA, V/Q scan, spirometry, HRCT, lung biopsy and point-of-care ultrasound. A V/Q scan is preferred over CTPA in contrast allergy and in pregnancy.
